questiontext.text: In an adjacency list representation of a graph, what does each vertex store?

answer.text: A list of its neighbouring (adjacent) vertices

feedback.text: Correct — each vertex keeps a list of the vertices it is directly connected to.

answer.text: A full V-length row of 0s and 1s for every other vertex

feedback.text: That describes a row of the adjacency matrix, not an adjacency list.

answer.text: Only its own degree as an integer

feedback.text: The degree alone does not tell you which vertices are neighbours.

answer.text: A pointer to the graph's root vertex

feedback.text: General graphs have no root, and that would not encode adjacency.

generalfeedback.text: An adjacency list gives each vertex a list of its neighbours, so it only stores edges that actually exist.

questiontext.text: What is the space complexity of an adjacency list for a graph with V vertices and E edges?

feedback.text: Correct — one entry per vertex plus one node per edge (or per endpoint).
That is the adjacency matrix's space, not the adjacency list's.
Storage grows linearly with edges, not quadratically.
You must store every vertex and edge, so it cannot be constant.

generalfeedback.text: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space: V list heads plus a node for each edge appearance.

questiontext.text: An adjacency list is most space-efficient for which kind of graph?

answer.text: A sparse graph, where E is far smaller than V^2

feedback.text: Correct — lists only store existing edges, ideal when edges are few.

answer.text: A dense graph, where E is close to V^2

feedback.text: For dense graphs a matrix is often preferable; lists lose their space advantage.

answer.text: A complete graph on every vertex

feedback.text: A complete graph is maximally dense — the worst case for adjacency-list savings.

answer.text: Any graph with exactly V^2 edges

feedback.text: That is a maximally dense graph, not where lists shine.

generalfeedback.text: Because it stores only real edges, an adjacency list shines on sparse graphs (E much smaller than V^2).

questiontext.text: Using an adjacency list, iterating over all neighbours of a vertex u costs:

feedback.text: Correct — you walk u's list, whose length is its degree.
That is the matrix cost; a list visits only actual neighbours.
You must visit each neighbour, so it depends on the degree.
You only traverse u's own list, not all edges in the graph.

generalfeedback.text: Neighbour iteration follows u's list, costing O(degree(u)) — a key advantage on sparse graphs.

questiontext.text: With an adjacency list, testing whether edge (u, v) exists takes O(degree(u)) time in the worst case.

feedback.text: Correct — you may have to scan all of u's neighbours.
An adjacency list has no O(1) edge lookup; you scan u's list.

questiontext.text: An adjacency list always uses less memory than an adjacency matrix, even for very dense graphs.

feedback.text: On dense graphs the per-node pointer overhead can exceed a compact matrix.
Correct — for dense graphs a matrix can be as good or better.

questiontext.text: In an adjacency list, the list attached to each vertex holds that vertex's ______ (the adjacent vertices).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about the adjacency-list representation are true? (select all that apply)

feedback.text: Yes — heads for V vertices plus one node per edge appearance.

answer.text: Iterating a vertex's neighbours costs O(degree)

feedback.text: Yes — you walk only that vertex's list.

answer.text: It supports O(1) worst-case edge existence tests

feedback.text: No — that is the adjacency matrix; a list must scan a vertex's neighbours.

answer.text: It uses O(V^2) space regardless of the number of edges

feedback.text: No — that is the matrix; a list's size scales with E.

generalfeedback.text: Adjacency lists: O(V + E) space, O(degree) neighbour scans, no O(1) edge test, and size scales with E (great for sparse graphs).
